title: Avalon Robotics — Private Interconnect & Onramp Intake
summary: Intro discovery about private connectivity options for Redwood Private. Avalon is evaluating Direct Connect/ExpressRoute + Transit Gateway model vs PrivateLink-style endpoints. Main drivers: data residency in EU, strict egress inspection, and predictable low latency for control-loop inference. Action items include network diagrams, sample throughput numbers, and a pilot run plan.
topics: KMS/HSM key separation and egress logs
next_steps: Redwood to share private-onramp checklist and security pack (SOC2 + network architecture) via Drive link
Priya to run a rough latency/bandwidth feasibility test and share csv
Customer to provide existing VPC CIDR ranges and NVA firewall constraints by 2028-08-07
Schedule technical pilot kickoff (30–45 min) week of 2028-08-14
action_items: Priya Shah: simulate 1k rps steady-state with 256 token average across us-west-2 -> eu-west-1 and report percentile latencies by 2028-08-09
Jordan Meyers: send pricing snapshot for Dedicated + private onramp options and pilot credit proposal by 2028-08-04
Samir Patel: export VPC topology and list of NVAs, subnets, and CIDRs; share split-horizon DNS requirements by 2028-08-07
Lena Ortiz: confirm compliance constraints (data-at-rest residency vs transferral) and send list of auditors by 2028-08-10
transcript:
[00:00:00] Jordan Meyers: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Jordan from Redwood.. good to see you, Avalon team. Quick roll call?
[00:00:08] Samir Patel: Samir here, cloud arch. Lena, Marcus, Olivia, Tori also here.
[00:00:14] Jordan Meyers: Great. Priya and Diego are with me on the call — Priya is our SE who will dive into network and infra stuff.
[00:00:20] Priya Shah: Hi all. I know you sent over some notes on the residency and inspection requirements, so we'll try to cover the options.
[00:00:27] Marcus Huang: Thanks. We want to understand what "Private" actually looks like. Our idea: no internet egress for inference traffic; everything over a direct private channel. Also EU residency for some models and logs.
[00:00:39] Priya Shah: Totally. At a high level we support a few patterns — aim is to match your network posture: 1) Transit Gateway / VPC peering — you peer your VPCs to Redwood-managed VPCs via Transit, or 2) Private endpoints (PrivateLink-style) where service endpoints are injected into your VPCs, or 3) Dedicated on‑prem appliance tunnels for air‑gapped. Most customers pick Transit for multi‑region routing flexibility but PrivateLink is used where tighter security controls or simpler IP planning is needed.
[00:01:06] Olivia Chen: Quick interruption — we run NVAs that require egress through a specific inspection appliance. If we do PrivateLink, how does traffic hit our NVA?
[00:01:14] Priya Shah: Good question. PrivateLink typically terminates in your subnet, so your regular route tables and inspection chain still apply — you'd need the endpoint ENI in a subnet that routes through the NVA. With Transit we use spokes and attachments, which sometimes lets you centralize egress inspection in a transit VPC. There are tradeoffs with hairpinning and cross‑AZ traffic.
[00:01:35] Samir Patel: And for cross‑region, we have EU and NA workloads. We need inference for control loops in NA but training/metrics in EU. Does Redwood allow region pinning per model or per route?
[00:01:46] Diego Alvarez: Yes — you can pin model versions and routes to regions. Our control plane can route by policy; for Private we can spin up model serving in the region you select or provide a fallback to the nearest compatible variant. That affects cost and latency.
[00:01:58] Lena Ortiz: On compliance: logs that include prompts must not leave EU, or must be redacted/encrypted with EU‑kept keys. How does KMS integration look when using Redwood Private?
[00:02:08] Priya Shah: For Private we support customer‑managed keys via KMS/HSM integrations. You control key policies; we never hold the plaintext keys. For log retention we can configure the private control plane to store audit logs in your region; if you choose Dedicated the storage can be customer‑owned. We'll send the security pack with specifics.
[00:02:22] Marcus Huang: What's the uplift to latency if we use a Private onramp versus hosting in the same VPC? We care about 95th percentile under 100ms ideally for the control loop.
[00:02:31] Priya Shah: It depends on where the serving nodes are and the overlay. If your app is in us-west-2 and the model is in eu-west-1 you'll see inter‑region latencies — that's why many customers run regional model replicas. For same‑region with PrivateLink, overhead is usually sub‑10ms added, but with Transit and centralized inspection you can add 5–30ms depending on path and NVA processing. We'll run some tests.
[00:02:53] Tori Evans: About IPs: we have limited /16 space per region. How do you handle IP exhaustion and endpoint IPs?
[00:03:00] Priya Shah: With PrivateLink endpoints we allocate ENIs in your subnets so you need available IPs there. For Transit attachments we can use AWS TGW route tables with specific prefixes; we typically recommend reserving a /24 per availability zone for endpoints. If IPs are constrained we have NAT gateway options or we can host endpoints in a dedicated subnet. We'll diagram this.
[00:03:18] Samir Patel: Egress costs: our finance team wants to understand predictable pricing. If we have high throughput inference cross-region, are we charged double egress?
[00:03:27] Jordan Meyers: Good callout. Egress depends on deployment mode. Hosted will have standard region egress; Dedicated can be negotiated in reserved‑capacity contracts with different cost profiles. For Private peering, cross‑region transfer is billed at cloud provider rates; Redwood can help architect to minimize transfer— e.g., keep serving in region or use caching/replicas. We'll include some sample math in pricing doc.
[00:03:46] Olivia Chen: We also route through an on‑prem firewall via Direct Connect. Can Redwood terminate over DX or ExpressRoute?
[00:03:54] Priya Shah: Yes. We work with Direct Connect/ExpressRoute by connecting via the customer's transit or partner connectivity. For Private deployments we can accept a BGP session into our transit fabric. There are options for private VIFs and partner routers. We do need the L3 adjacency details and ASN plan.
[00:04:09] Lena Ortiz: What about mutual TLS and client certs between our app and the Redwood endpoint?
[00:04:14] Diego Alvarez: We support mTLS for service-to-service. For PrivateLink endpoints we can require TLS with client certs issued by your CA, or we can integrate with an mTLS gateway. We'll capture the handshake requirements.
[00:04:26] Marcus Huang: Are there any managed NAT requirements? Our NVAs require ephemeral outbound connections to 3rd party sanity checks; would that break the "no internet egress" rule?
[00:04:34] Priya Shah: You can keep control/eval traffic internal while allowing specific egress for approved external services through your NVA. Redwood's routes can be configured so that inference traffic stays private while other allowed flows egress. We'll need to capture your allowlist.
[00:04:47] Samir Patel: On monitoring: we need per‑token latency and trace spans forwarded to our X‑Apm collector but without sending prompt text. Is that feasible?
[00:04:56] Diego Alvarez: Absolutely. We have token‑level metrics and can redact or hash prompt text before forwarding. We also provide token‑level cost breakdowns. For Private deployments we can forward traces to your collector over private peering.
[00:05:09] Tori Evans: Do you have a reference architecture for a Transit Gateway design that centralizes inspection and supports multi‑region redundancies?
[00:05:16] Priya Shah: Yes — we'll attach a diagram. Common pattern: TGW in primary region with spokes for app VPCs, Redwood managed attachment, and centralized NVAs in a security VPC with route propagation. Secondary region has failover replicas and synced model versions. We'll send the doc and a checklist of required route tables and NACLs.
[00:05:31] Lena Ortiz: Audit logging: we need an immutable record of model invocations for 2 years. Can you store logs in our S3 bucket using cross‑account write with SSE‑KMS?
[00:05:40] Diego Alvarez: Yes — cross‑account S3 puts with SSE‑KMS are supported. We'll provide the IAM role and bucket policy templates. For extra assurance we can ship logs to your SIEM over private forwarding.
[00:05:51] Marcus Huang: How does fallback work if a pinned region is overloaded? Do you allow degraded models in the same language family?
[00:05:58] Priya Shah: Exactly. Routing policies can include fallbacks to compatible model variants in other regions or smaller quantized variants. We also support canary rollouts and automatic fallback to hosted public endpoints if desired.
[00:06:10] Olivia Chen: Any restrictions on ports or protocols for Private endpoints?
[00:06:14] Priya Shah: Standard TLS on 443, mTLS options, and for telemetry we use a configurable port range. No UDP. We'll provide a network port matrix.
[00:06:22] Samir Patel: Performance testing — can Redwood run a pilot with a 2‑week ramp, starting 100rps to 1k rps with our model and dataset?
[00:06:30] Jordan Meyers: We offer pilot programs — usually 2–4 weeks. For pilots we can provide reserved pilot capacity on Dedicated or a scoped hosted setup. Priya will scope the test here.
[00:06:37] Priya Shah: For the pilot we need: sample request payload sizes (avg tokens), concurrency pattern, target p95, and any special NVA traffic shaping. We'll do a smoke test and then a ramp, capturing p50/p95/p99 and token cost.
[00:06:49] Tori Evans: Ok. Can we talk about DNS? We use split‑horizon for internal names. Private endpoints need to resolve internally — will Redwood provide private hosted zone records?
[00:06:57] Diego Alvarez: We can push private DNS entries to your Route 53 private hosted zone or provide CNAMEs that you control. There are two models: you own the namespace or Redwood manages internal records in a delegated zone. We'll document both.
[00:07:10] Samir Patel: Anything else on security? We're looking for SAML SSO, RBAC, and least privilege for operators.
[00:07:17] Jordan Meyers: All supported. SSO via SAML/OIDC, RBAC roles, per‑token scoping for apps, plus audit trails. We'll include the SSO setup guide.
[00:07:24] Lena Ortiz: Let's recap the blockers: 1) IP space and endpoint planning; 2) NVA path and inspection constraints; 3) EU log residency and KMS; 4) pilot sizing and timeline.
[00:07:35] Jordan Meyers: Good recap. Any questions from the customer side before we wrap?
[00:07:40] Marcus Huang: One more — we sometimes use on‑prem GPUs with our own scheduler. Can Redwood federate to an on‑prem cluster?
[00:07:47] Priya Shah: We have private deployment options that integrate with customer on‑prem via secure tunnels. For tightly-coupled on‑prem serving you may need the on‑prem package; we'd coordinate a connectivity runbook.
[00:07:58] Olivia Chen: OK great. We'll share our VPC export and NVA config.
[00:08:03] Jordan Meyers: We'll send the security pack, deployment checklist, and pilot proposal after this call. Priya — anything else?
[00:08:09] Priya Shah: I'll follow up with a pilot scoping doc and a quick latency test plan.
[00:08:14] Samir Patel: Perfect. Thanks everyone.
[00:08:17] Jordan Meyers: Thanks all — meeting adjourned.
